'''Mehtaab Sawhney''' (born September 20, 1998){{cn|date=May 2026}} is an American mathematician, specializing in [[combinatorics]] and [[number theory]]. He is an assistant professor at [[Columbia University]].

== Early life and education ==
Sawhney grew up in [[Commack, New York|Commack]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. While attending [[Commack School District|Commack High School]], Sawhney competed in the [[United States of America Mathematical Olympiad]] (USAMO), and participated in [[MIT PRIMES]].<ref name = "mit news">{{cite web|last=Mongo|first=Julia|date=January 30, 2020|title=Mehtaab Sawhney named 2020 Churchill Scholar|url=https://news.mit.edu/2020/mehtaab-sawhney-named-churchill-scholar-0130|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[MIT News]]}}</ref> In 2016, for his research in graph theory through MIT PRIMES, he was named a semifinalist in the [[Regeneron Science Talent Search|Intel Science Talent Search]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Intel STS 2016 semifinalists|url=https://www.societyforscience.org/regeneron-sts/intel-sts-2016-semifinalists/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[Society for Science]]}}</ref> and won an award at the [[International Science and Engineering Fair]].<ref>{{cite web|date=May 13, 2016|title=Intel ISEF 2016 Grand Award winners|url=https://www.societyforscience.org/press-release/intel-isef-2016-grand-award-winners/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[Society for Science]]}}</ref>

Sawhney attended the [[University of Pennsylvania]] for one year before transferring to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he studied mathematics and computer science.<ref name = "mit news"/> He received an honorable mention in the [[Putnam Competition]] in 2016, 2018, and 2019.<ref name = "mit news"/> In 2020, he was awarded a [[Churchill Scholarship]] for further study in mathematics at [[Cambridge University]], after which he returned to MIT for doctoral studies. With his frequent collaborator [[Ashwin Sah]], he received an honorable mention for the [[Morgan Prize]] for undergraduate research in 2020,<ref>{{cite web|date=November 20, 2019|title=Nina Zubrilina to receive the 2020 Morgan Prize|url=https://maa.org/news/nina-zubrilina-to-receive-the-2020-morgan-prize/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[Mathematical Association of America]]}}</ref> and won the Morgan Prize in 2021.<ref>{{cite web|date=October 29, 2020|title=Ashwin Sah and Mehtaab Sawhney receive 2021 Morgan Prize|url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=6435|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[American Mathematical Society]]}}</ref> He completed his PhD in 2024, supervised by Yufei Zhao.<ref name = "clay">{{cite web|date=July 1, 2024|title=Mehtaab Sawhney|url=https://www.claymath.org/people/mehtaab-sawhney/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[Clay Mathematics Institute]]}}</ref>

== Career ==
At MIT, Sawhney was noted for his productive collaboration with fellow student [[Ashwin Sah]] in the fields of [[combinatorics]] and [[number theory]]. Sah and Sawhney each attended MIT for undergraduate and doctoral studies between 2017 and 2024. During that time, they co-authored more than 50 papers,<ref name = "quanta szemeredi">{{cite news|last=Sloman|first=Leila|date=August 5, 2024|title=Grad students find inevitable patterns in big sets of numbers|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/grad-students-find-inevitable-patterns-in-big-sets-of-numbers-20240805/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref> on topics such as [[Ramsey theory]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Hartnett|first=Kevin|date=November 30, 2020|title=Undergraduate math student pushes frontier of graph theory|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mit-undergraduate-math-student-pushes-frontier-of-graph-theory-20201130/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref> [[Steiner system]]s,<ref>{{cite news|last=Sloman|first=Leila|date=July 14, 2022|title=Hypergraphs reveal solution to 50-year-old problem|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/hypergraphs-reveal-solution-to-50-year-old-problem-20220714/|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref> subspace designs,<ref>{{cite news|last=Cepelewicz|first=Jordana|date=April 12, 2023|title=Mathematicians find hidden structure in a common type of space|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-find-hidden-structure-in-a-common-type-of-space-20230412/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref> and [[Szemerédi's theorem]].<ref name = "quanta szemeredi"/>

In 2024, Sawhney collaborated with [[Ben Green (mathematician)|Ben Green]] to prove that, for any ''n'' ≡ 0, 4 (mod 6), there are infinitely many prime numbers of the form ''p''<sup>2</sup> + ''nq''<sup>2</sup>, where ''p'' and ''q'' are themselves constrained to be prime numbers. The case ''n'' = 4 resolved a conjecture made by [[John Friedlander]] and [[Henryk Iwaniec]] in 2018.<ref>{{cite news|last=Howlett|first=Joseph|date=December 11, 2024|title=Mathematicians uncover a new way to count prime numbers|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-uncover-a-new-way-to-count-prime-numbers-20241211/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref>

Sawhney was awarded a [[Clay Mathematics Institute|Clay Research Fellowship]] in 2024,<ref name = "clay"/> and a [[David and Lucile Packard Foundation|Packard Fellowship]] in 2025.<ref>{{cite web|date=October 15, 2025|title=The David and Lucile Packard Foundation announces the 2025 Class of Packard Fellows for Science and Engineering|url=https://www.packard.org/insights/news/the-david-and-lucile-packard-foundation-announces-the-2025-class-of-packard-fellows-for-science-and-engineering/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[David and Lucile Packard Foundation]]}}</ref> He became a tenure-track assistant professor of mathematics at [[Columbia University]] in 2024. He went on leave from Columbia in 2026 to join the artificial intelligence company [[OpenAI]] as a mathematician.<ref name = "sci am feb 2026">{{cite news|last=Howlett|first=Joseph|date=February 12, 2026|title=Is AI on the precipice of revolutionizing math? It depends|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ai-uncovers-solutions-to-erdos-problems-moving-closer-to-transforming-math/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Scientific American]]}}</ref>

In 2025, Sawhney and Mark Sellke used [[GPT-5]], a [[large language model]] developed by OpenAI, to search the literature on several [[List of conjectures by Paul Erdős|conjectures made by Paul Erdős]] in combinatorial number theory.<ref name = "sci am feb 2026"/><ref>{{cite web|date=November 20, 2025|title=Early experiments in accelerating science with GPT-5|url=https://openai.com/index/accelerating-science-gpt-5/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|website=[[OpenAI]]}}</ref> In 2026, Sawhney and Sellke used GPT-5 to find a counterexample to Erdős's conjecture on [[unit distance graph]]s.<ref>{{cite news|last=Howlett|first=Joseph|date=May 21, 2026|title=OpenAI announces AI's biggest math breakthrough yet|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ai-just-solved-an-80-year-old-erdos-problem-and-mathematicians-are-amazed/|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[Scientific American]]}}</ref> GPT-5 provided a method to construct ''n'' points in the plane from which ''[[Big O notation#Vinogradov's ≫ and Knuth's big Ω|Ω]]''(''n''<sup>1+''ε''</sup>) pairs of points are unit distance apart, for some ''ε'' > 0.<ref name = "sawin">{{cite arxiv|last=Sawin|first=Will|author-link=Will Sawin|date=May 20, 2026|title=An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem|eprint=2605.20579|class=math.CO}}</ref> A team of mathematicians simplified the argument and computed an explicit lower bound for the exponent ''ε'' to be 6 × 10<sup>−38</sup>; [[Will Sawin]] subsequently improved the exponent to ''ε'' ≈ 0.014.<ref name = "sawin"/> The construction is motivated by [[algebraic number theory]], in particular the [[Golod–Shafarevich theorem]], and involves high-dimensional lattices arising from [[CM-field]]s.<ref name = "sawin"/> [[Timothy Gowers]] hailed the result as "a milestone in [[Applications of artificial intelligence#Mathematics|AI mathematics]]".<ref>{{cite news|last=Milmo|first=Dan|last2=Sample|first2=Ian|date=May 21, 2026|title=OpenAI makes breakthrough on 80-year-old maths problem|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/may/21/openai-paul-erdos-maths-problem-breakthrough|url-status=live|access-date=May 22, 2026|work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref>

In September 2026, Sawhney and Mark Sellke disclosed that they had utilized OpenAI's reasoning models (notably the [[GPT-6 Astra|Astra]] model) to resolve several long-standing open problems in pure mathematics.<ref name="a16z_podcast_2026" /> Among the most significant results was a breakthrough in [[Sphere packing#Hypersphere packing|high-dimensional sphere packing]]. Through a new connection between spherical codes and full-space packings utilizing [[representation theory]], the models established a strict improvement over the 1970s linear programming bound, achieving an asymptotic value of <math>e^{-(2\pi + o(1))d}</math> (roughly <math>2^{-0.61d}</math>).<ref name="marginal_revolution_2026" /> 

Additionally, Sawhney and Sellke reported that the AI system successfully generated a 15-page proof confirming the existence of a [[Sofic group#Existence of non-sofic groups|non-sofic group]], resolving a major open question in [[group theory]].<ref name="a16z_podcast_2026" /> Discussing the impact of frontier AI on the field, Sawhney noted that the models exhibit reasoning traces similar to human mathematicians, including the ability to independently backtrack on failed approaches. He observed that as AI accelerates mathematical discovery, the primary bottleneck for human mathematicians is shifting from generating proofs to absorbing and contextualizing AI-generated mathematics.<ref name="a16z_podcast_2026" />
